newsitem.title: PERU: Fear of false move hangs over 20-day Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Fear of false move hangs over 20-day Peru siege.

text.p: The threat of a bloody end to Peru's deadlocked hostage crisis hung over the heads of 74 captives on Monday amid fears that one false move by the government or guerrillas could trigger the use of force.
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned the 20-day standoff at his ambassador's besieged residence in Lima could get out of hand.

"It will be a protracted battle and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," he told reporters. "There have been miscues on the guerrillas' side and also on the Peruvian government's side," he added without elaborating.

The heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were vigilant for a possible attack by Peruvian security forces. Guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was moving constantly around the building, using important hostages such as Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela as a "human shield" to avoid being a target, according to a local daily.

Miles above, Peruvian intelligence officials used a satellite to track movements inside the residence, Expreso reported. The images showed the guerrillas operating a rotation system allowing five of them to sleep at any one time, for four hours each day.

There was no sign of government negotiator Domingo Palermo, the Education Minister, who has not entered the booby-trapped and mined residence since a first face-to-face meeting nine days ago. Nor did the Red Cross' Michel Minnig, the chief mediator in the crisis, or Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, an observer and close friend of President Alberto Fujimori, appear there.

The rebels have freed no hostages since New Year's Day. The end to the regular releases under which more than 430 captives were freed has prompted the Red Cross to call for patience on both sides as the siege drags toward its third week.

While Japan has constantly urged Peru to look for a peaceful solution to the crisis, Fujimori, who is of Japanese extraction, has adamantly rejected ruling out force until all hostages are released and the guerrillas lay down their arms.

Japan's Hashimoto has expressed fears that a dramatic rescue attempt could cause bloodshed -- especially because the jungle-trained guerrillas can control their captives more easily as their number has fallen with successive releases.

The rebels are widely believed to number about 20 but the Red Cross has fuelled speculation there could be more after revealing the organisation provides those inside the residence with 110 portions for each meal -- 16 more than thought necessary.

While the ambassador's residence is technically Japanese territory, Tokyo has ceded control over the siege to Fujimori. Hashimoto, who cancelled New Year plans so he could monitor the hostage crisis, on Tuesday will begin a trip to five Southeast Asian countries, a move officials said reflected Japan's confidence in Fujimori.

This support for Fujimori was echoed in Lima by Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar who spent Monday in a series of meetings with Peruvian government officials to try to help bring about a solution. Bolivia's captive ambassador Jorge Gumucio is the only remaining hostage not from Peru or Japan.

With Tudela held hostage, acting Foreign Minister Jorge Gonzales Izquierdo accompanied Aranibar as he sped around Lima on his frenetic diploamtic mission. At a news conference on Sunday, the Bolivian minister backed Fujimori's uncompromising position and ruled out releasing four MRTA prisoners in Bolivia.

The MRTA has demanded the release of all their 400-odd jailed comrades in return for freeing their VIP hostages, who include Fujimori's brother, Pedro, top government and security force officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
The rebels took their glittering haul on Dec. 17 when they burst in on a cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday that was attended by more than 500 people.
